usage: Pairs with 씻다 (rinse with water), the default verb for dishes — not 닦다.
그릇 is a productive suffix: 밥그릇 (rice), 국그릇 (soup), 개밥그릇 (dog's bowl).
Use the location particle 에 plus 담다 (to put food in) — the natural pair for filling a bowl.
그릇 is the typical thing you 깨다 (break/smash); 깨진 그릇 = a broken bowl.
examples: 그릇이 예뻐요.
The bowl is pretty.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + descriptive adjective 예쁘다.
밥을 그릇에 담아 주세요.
Please serve the rice into a bowl.
Everyday request: location 에 + 담다, the verb for putting food in.
설거지할 때 깨지기 쉬운 그릇은 따로 씻으세요.
When you do the dishes, wash fragile bowls separately.
Real situation: 깨지기 쉽다 (easy to break) modifying 그릇 in a kitchen instruction.
nuance: 그릇 is the broad native-Korean word for a vessel that holds food — most often the deeper, rounded bowl that rice, soup, or 반찬 sit in, but it also works as the generic cover term for 'dishes/dishware' (그릇을 닦다 = do the dishes). The dividing line you must feel is 그릇 vs 접시: 그릇 is deep and holds something pourable or piled, while 접시 is the flat plate you lay food onto. Note the everyday verb is 씻다 (rinse), not the English-driven 닦다 (wipe) — 닦다 is for wiping a surface dry, not washing dishes. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you serve food 그릇에 담다 (into the bowl, location 에), so saying 그릇을 담다 is wrong because 담다 needs the destination, not the food, marked. Common collocations: 그릇을 씻다, 그릇에 담다, 그릇을 깨다, 밥그릇.

mistakes: Don't say 그릇을 닦아요 for washing dishes. 닦다 means to wipe (a table, a window) — washing dishes with water is 그릇을 씻어요 / 설거지를 해요.
Don't say 밥을 그릇을 담아요. The bowl is the destination, so it takes 에: 밥을 그릇에 담아요. Marking the bowl with 을 makes the sentence ungrammatical.
Don't reach for 보울 (a borrowed 'bowl'). Korean uses the native 그릇; the loanword sounds unnatural for a normal eating bowl.

usage: to plate / put onto a plate
Location 에 + 담다; food lands ON a flat 접시, so 에 is required, never 를.
Flat dishes are counted with 장 (sheet-counter) as well as 개; 종이 한 장 uses the same counter.
앞 (front) + 접시 = the small plate set in front of each diner to take shared food onto.
치우다 (clear away) is the natural verb for taking dirty 접시 off the table after a meal.
examples: 접시가 더러워요.
The plate is dirty.
Simple frame: subject 이 + adjective 더럽다.
과일을 접시에 예쁘게 담았어요.
I arranged the fruit nicely on the plate.
Everyday: location 에 + 담다 with the adverb 예쁘게.
손님이 오시니까 앞접시도 함께 놓아 주세요.
Since guests are coming, please also set out individual plates.
Real situation: hosting context introducing 앞접시 and honorific 오시다.
nuance: 접시 is a flat, shallow plate — the dish you LAY food onto (fruit, grilled meat, a slice of cake) rather than pour into. The contrast to lock in is 접시 vs 그릇: shape decides it, not the food itself. A flat dish is 접시 even for soup-adjacent food, while anything deep and rounded is 그릇. A useful sub-word is 앞접시, the small personal plate each diner pulls shared dishes onto — a normal part of Korean table manners. Because food sits ON the surface, the particle is 접시에 담다 / 접시에 놓다 (location 에); the classic English-speaker error is 접시를 담다, treating the plate as the object. Note plates can be counted with 장 (the sheet-counter, reflecting their flatness) as well as the all-purpose 개. Habitual collocations: 접시에 담다, 접시를 치우다, 접시를 깨다, 앞접시.

mistakes: Don't say 과일을 접시를 담아요. The plate is where the fruit goes, so use 에: 과일을 접시에 담아요.
Don't assume soup goes on a 접시. Liquid or piled food needs the deeper 그릇; a flat 접시 is for things you lay flat, like meat or fruit.
Don't always default to 개 when counting. Flat plates are often counted with 장 — 접시 두 장 — which sounds more natural to many speakers.

usage: Location 에 + 따르다 (pour); the liquid's destination is the cup, marked with 에.
컵 compounds freely: 종이컵 (paper), 머그컵 (mug), 텀블러 is separate but related.
When measuring a drink, the counter is 잔 (glass/cupful): 물 한 잔, 커피 두 잔.
헹구다 (rinse out) is the precise verb for quickly washing a drinking cup with water.
examples: 컵이 깨끗해요.
The cup is clean.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.
컵에 물을 따라 주세요.
Please pour water into the cup.
Everyday request: destination 에 + 따르다 for pouring a drink.
뜨거우니까 종이컵 말고 머그컵에 드릴게요.
Since it's hot, I'll give it to you in a mug, not a paper cup.
Real situation: contrasting 종이컵/머그컵 with 말고 (not ~ but) and honorific 드리다.
nuance: 컵 is a loanword (from English 'cup') covering both cups and drinking glasses for any beverage — there is no everyday split between 'cup' and 'glass' the way English makes one; a glass tumbler and a coffee cup are both 컵 in normal speech, with 머그컵 (mug) and 종이컵 (paper cup) as specific compounds. Watch the difference between the OBJECT and the MEASURE: 컵 is the physical cup, but when you order or count a serving of a drink you switch to the counter 잔 — 커피 한 잔, not 커피 한 컵 in a café. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with pouring: you pour a drink 컵에 따르다 (into the cup, location 에), so 컵을 따르다 is wrong. Also use 따르다 (pour) rather than the English-shaped 붓다, which sounds like dumping a large amount. Frequent collocations: 컵에 따르다, 컵을 헹구다, 종이컵, 머그컵.

mistakes: Don't order 커피 한 컵 in a café. Servings of drinks use the counter 잔: 커피 한 잔. 컵 names the object, not the portion.
Don't say 물을 컵을 따라요. The cup is the destination of the pour, so it takes 에: 물을 컵에 따라요.
Don't worry about 'cup vs glass.' Korean 컵 covers both; you don't need a separate word for a drinking glass in everyday speech.

usage: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up); the spoon is the tool, so 으로 is required.
숟가락 + 젓가락 together = 수저, the standard table-setting pair Koreans lay out.
to set down / lay out a spoon
놓다 = set the spoon on the table; idiomatically 숟가락을 놓다 can also mean 'finish eating.'
밥 + 숟가락; also used figuratively for a mouthful, as in 한 숟가락만 더.
examples: 숟가락이 없어요.
There's no spoon.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.
국을 숟가락으로 떠서 먹어요.
I scoop the soup with a spoon and eat it.
Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, linked to 먹다 with -서.
밥 다 먹었으면 숟가락 놓고 잠깐 쉬자.
If you're done eating, put down your spoon and rest a bit.
Real situation: casual 반말 with the idiom 숟가락(을) 놓다 = stop eating.
nuance: 숟가락 is the deep-bowled metal spoon at the heart of a Korean table — Koreans eat rice and especially soup/stew with it, unlike many cultures that treat the spoon as secondary to the fork. Pair it with the verb 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid or rice), the precise partner verb. Crucially, 숟가락 + 젓가락 combine into 수저, the everyday word for the whole utensil set you lay out — if someone says 수저 놓아 줘, they mean set out both. A spelling trap: it's 숟가락 with ㄷ (a historical 술 'spoon' + 가락), even though 젓가락 takes ㅅ — learners often wrongly write 숫가락. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you eat 숟가락으로 (with a spoon, instrument 으로), never 숟가락에. Watch the idiom 숟가락을 놓다 — literally 'put down the spoon,' it commonly means to finish a meal. Collocations: 숟가락으로 뜨다, 숟가락을 놓다, 수저, 밥숟가락.

mistakes: Don't write 숫가락. The correct spelling is 숟가락 with ㄷ; only 젓가락 uses ㅅ. They differ on purpose.
Don't say 숟가락에 먹어요. The spoon is the instrument, so it takes 으로: 숟가락으로 먹어요.
Don't take 숟가락을 놓다 literally every time. Beyond 'set the spoon down,' it idiomatically means 'finish eating,' so context matters.

usage: Instrument 으로 + 집다 (grasp/pick up) — the precise verb for what chopsticks do.
Noun + 질 (doing-an-action) = handling chopsticks; 젓가락질이 서툴다 = clumsy with chopsticks.
나무 (wood) + 젓가락; the throwaway kind from a 분식집, vs everyday metal ones.
Paired utensils take the counter 벌 (set); 한 짝 = just one stick of the pair.
examples: 젓가락이 어려워요.
Chopsticks are hard.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 어렵다.
반찬을 젓가락으로 집어서 먹어요.
I pick up side dishes with chopsticks and eat them.
Everyday: instrument 으로 + 집다, chained to 먹다 with -서.
젓가락질이 아직 서툴러서 면이 자꾸 미끄러져요.
My chopstick skill is still clumsy, so the noodles keep slipping.
Real situation: 젓가락질 + 서투르다 (르-irregular), explaining a genuine struggle.
nuance: 젓가락 is chopsticks — and Korean chopsticks are distinctively flat, heavy METAL ones, harder for beginners than the rounded wooden chopsticks of Japan or China. The partner verb is 집다 (to grasp/pick up), the action chopsticks perform; for noodles 면을 집다 is natural. A high-value derived word is 젓가락질, 'the skill/act of using chopsticks' (the 질 suffix = doing an action), so 젓가락질이 서툴다 = to be clumsy with chopsticks. Remember 젓가락 takes ㅅ while its partner 숟가락 takes ㄷ — don't cross them. Together they form 수저, the utensil set. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: the particle is 젓가락으로 (instrument 으로), not 젓가락에; and because the word is already plural in meaning, you don't pluralize it — to count, use 벌 for a pair (한 벌) or 짝 for a single stick. Collocations: 젓가락으로 집다, 젓가락질, 나무젓가락, 젓가락 한 벌.

mistakes: Don't write 젇가락 or 저가락. The standard spelling is 젓가락 with ㅅ; pair it correctly against 숟가락 (ㄷ).
Don't say 젓가락에 먹어요. Chopsticks are the instrument: 젓가락으로 먹어요.
Don't count chopsticks with 개 as if singular. A usable pair is 한 벌; a single stick is 한 짝 — 개 sounds off for paired utensils.

usage: Instrument 으로 + 찍다 (stab/spear) — the signature fork action for fruit or cake.
Loanword counted simply with 개/하나; 포크 하나 주세요 = please give me one fork.
In Western-dining contexts the knife is the loanword 나이프, paired with 포크 (vs native 칼).
일회용 (single-use) + 포크; the plastic kind handed out with takeout food.
examples: 포크가 없어요.
There's no fork.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.
케이크를 포크로 찍어서 먹어요.
I spear the cake with a fork and eat it.
Everyday: instrument 으로 + 찍다, the natural verb for forking cake.
아이는 아직 젓가락이 서툴러서 포크로 먹는 게 편해요.
The child is still clumsy with chopsticks, so eating with a fork is easier.
Real situation: contrasting 젓가락/포크 with the nominalizer -는 게.
nuance: 포크 is a loanword (English 'fork') and in Korea is a SECONDARY, situational utensil — used for cake, fruit, salad, and Western food, while everyday rice and soup go with 숟가락 and 젓가락. Its natural partner verb is 찍다 (to stab/spear), as in 과일을 포크로 찍다; this 찍다 also means 'to stamp/take a photo,' so context disambiguates. In a Western place-setting the fork pairs with the loanword 나이프, whereas the all-purpose Korean kitchen knife is the native 칼 — so 포크와 나이프 (table setting) but 칼 (cooking). The English-speaker pitfall is, as with all tools, the particle: 포크로 먹다 (instrument 으로), never 포크에. Don't over-use 포크 — defaulting to a fork at a Korean meal of rice and 반찬 reads as foreign; reach for 젓가락 instead. Collocations: 포크로 찍다, 포크와 나이프, 일회용 포크, 포크 하나.

usage: Instrument 으로 + 썰다 (slice into pieces) — the core knife action in cooking.
the knife cuts well / is sharp
Idiom: 들다 here means 'cuts well'; 안 든다 = it's dull. Not the 들다 'to hold.'
과도 (果刀, fruit-knife) is the small knife for peeling fruit, a specific type of 칼.
갈다 (grind/sharpen) is the verb for putting an edge back on a dull blade.
examples: 칼이 날카로워요.
The knife is sharp.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 날카롭다 (ㅂ-irregular).
채소를 칼로 얇게 썰어요.
I slice the vegetables thinly with a knife.
Everyday: instrument 으로 + 썰다 with the adverb 얇게.
이 칼은 잘 안 드니까 한번 갈아야겠어요.
This knife doesn't cut well, so I'd better sharpen it.
Real situation: the idiom 안 들다 (dull) + resolve ending -아야겠다.
nuance: 칼 is the native, all-purpose Korean word for a knife — above all the kitchen knife, but the SAME word covers any blade: a pocketknife, a sword, a box cutter, all 칼. So unlike English, you don't switch words by type; you specify with a modifier (부엌칼 kitchen, 과도 fruit knife, 맥가이버 칼 Swiss-army). Two idioms are essential: 칼이 잘 들다 means 'the knife cuts well / is sharp' — here 들다 is NOT 'to hold' but 'to cut/take effect,' so 칼이 안 들어요 = it's dull; and 칼을 갈다 = to sharpen. The partner cutting verbs are 썰다 (slice into pieces) and 자르다 (cut through). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 칼로 썰다 (instrument 으로), never 칼에. Note that in a Western table setting the table knife is the loanword 나이프, not 칼. Collocations: 칼로 썰다, 칼이 들다, 칼을 갈다, 과도.

Don't expect a different word for sword vs kitchen knife. Korean uses 칼 for both and adds a modifier (부엌칼, 과도) when the type matters.

usage: Location 에 + 끓이다; the cooking happens IN the pot, so 에 marks it, not 를.
받침 (support) — the mat you rest a hot 냄비 on so it doesn't burn the table.
Note: a rice/pressure cooker is 솥, a different (heavier, lidded) vessel from 냄비.
for food to scorch onto the pot
눌어붙다 = stick-and-burn to the bottom; a common kitchen mishap with 냄비.
examples: 냄비가 뜨거워요.
The pot is hot.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular).
라면은 작은 냄비에 끓이면 더 맛있어요.
Ramen tastes better cooked in a small pot.
Everyday: location 에 + 끓이다 with the conditional -면.
냄비가 뜨거우니까 꼭 받침 위에 올려놓으세요.
Since the pot is hot, be sure to set it on a trivet.
Real situation: reason -니까 + 냄비 받침 in a safety instruction.
nuance: 냄비 is a relatively light cooking pot or saucepan — the everyday vessel for boiling soup, simmering 찌개, or making ramen. Two contrasts matter: 냄비 vs 솥 — 솥 is the heavier, deep, lidded cauldron/cooker (think 가마솥, 압력솥 for rice), so don't call a rice cooker a 냄비; and 냄비 vs 프라이팬 — the flat frying pan is its own loanword. The partner verb is 끓이다 (to boil/cook by boiling), and food that scorches onto the bottom 눌어붙다. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you cook 냄비에 끓이다 (location 에) — saying 냄비를 끓이다 literally means 'boil the pot itself,' which is wrong; the pot is where it happens, the food is the object (라면을 냄비에 끓이다). Culturally note 냄비 근성 ('a pot temperament') — a set phrase for quick-to-boil, quick-to-cool enthusiasm. Collocations: 냄비에 끓이다, 냄비 받침, 냄비가 눌어붙다, 냄비 뚜껑.

usage: Action location 에서 + 먹다; an action happens AT the table, so 에서, not 에.
차리다 = lay out a meal/setting; 식탁을 차리다 / 밥상을 차리다 = prepare the table.
위 (top) pins location to the surface: 식탁 위에 그릇이 있다.
식탁 + 보 (cloth wrap) = the cloth spread over the dining table.
examples: 식탁이 커요.
The dining table is big.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 크다.
가족이 식탁에 둘러앉아서 밥을 먹어요.
The family sits around the table and eats.
Everyday: 둘러앉다 (sit around) + the action verb 먹다.
저녁 다 됐으니까 얼른 식탁 좀 차려 줄래?
Dinner's ready, so could you set the table quickly?
Real situation: casual request -어 줄래? with 식탁을 차리다.
nuance: 식탁 is Sino-Korean, 食卓 — 食 'eat/food' + 卓 'table,' literally an 'eating-table,' i.e. the dining table. Distinguish it from 책상 (a desk, 冊床 'book-table' for study/work) and from 밥상, the lower, often portable meal-table (and by extension the whole spread of food) of more traditional dining — 밥상 emphasizes the laid meal, 식탁 the piece of furniture. The everyday verb is 식탁을 차리다 (set/lay the table). The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an ACTION done at the table uses 에서, so 식탁에서 밥을 먹다 — using 식탁에 먹다 is wrong because 에 marks static location/existence (식탁에 그릇이 있다), while 에서 marks where an action occurs. To pin something to the surface, add 위: 식탁 위에 놓다. Collocations: 식탁에서 먹다, 식탁을 차리다, 식탁 위, 식탁보.

Don't say 식탁을 만들어요 to mean 'set the table.' Use 차리다: 식탁을 차려요. 만들다 = build the furniture, not lay the meal.

usage: Action location 에서 + 요리하다; cooking is an action, so 에서, not 에.
용품 (goods/supplies) — 주방 용품 = the pots, knives, and tools of a kitchen.
Real-estate/café term for a kitchen open to the dining area; 주방 takes many such modifiers.
주방 + 장 (長, head) = the chef in charge of a restaurant kitchen.
examples: 주방이 넓어요.
The kitchen is spacious.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 넓다.
엄마가 주방에서 저녁을 만들고 계세요.
Mom is making dinner in the kitchen.
Everyday: action location 에서 + honorific progressive -고 계시다.
식당 주방은 위생이 생명이라 늘 깨끗하게 관리해요.
A restaurant kitchen lives or dies by hygiene, so it's always kept clean.
Real situation: 주방 in a professional sense with 위생/관리하다.
nuance: 주방 is Sino-Korean, 廚房 — 廚 'kitchen' + 房 'room,' literally the 'kitchen room.' The register contrast you should feel is 주방 vs 부엌: both name the cooking room, but 주방 is the slightly more formal, modern, and PROFESSIONAL-leaning word (a restaurant kitchen, kitchenware ads, 주방장 head chef, an apartment's '오픈 주방'), while 부엌 is the warm, homey native word for the kitchen at home — many speakers use them interchangeably for a home kitchen, but you'd never say a restaurant's 부엌 in a business context. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: cooking is an action, so 주방에서 요리하다 (action location 에서), not 주방에 요리하다 — 에 is only for existence (주방에 냉장고가 있다). Useful derivations: 주방 용품 (kitchenware), 주방장 (head chef). Collocations: 주방에서 요리하다, 주방 용품, 오픈 주방, 주방장.

usage: to cut on the cutting board
위 + action location 에서; you cut ON TOP of the board, so 위에서, not bare 에.
to wipe the board with a cloth
Here 닦다 (wipe) is right — wiping the board's surface, vs 씻다 for rinsing it.
나무 (wood) vs 플라스틱 도마 (plastic); material modifiers are common with 도마.
the sound of chopping (on the board)
도마 소리 evokes the rhythmic knock of cooking; a vivid everyday collocation.
examples: 도마가 깨끗해요.
The cutting board is clean.
Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.
채소를 도마 위에서 썰어요.
I slice the vegetables on the cutting board.
Everyday: 도마 위에서 + 썰다, the standard chopping frame.
고기랑 채소는 도마를 따로 써야 위생적이에요.
It's more hygienic to use separate boards for meat and vegetables.
Real situation: 따로 쓰다 (use separately) + 위생적이다 in a kitchen-safety tip.
nuance: 도마 is the cutting board — the flat surface you set food on to chop with a 칼. There isn't a tricky near-synonym; the value is in the GRAMMAR and collocations. Because cutting happens on top of the board's surface, the natural frame is 도마 위에서 썰다 (위 'top' + action-location 에서) — bare 도마에 썰다 sounds incomplete, since 에 marks static existence, not where an action plays out. Note the two cleaning verbs split by sense: 도마를 씻다 = rinse it with water; 도마를 닦다 = wipe its surface — both valid, unlike with dishes where 닦다 was wrong. Korean kitchens commonly keep separate boards (고기용/채소용) for hygiene, so 도마를 따로 쓰다 is a natural phrase. Material modifiers abound: 나무 도마, 플라스틱 도마. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 위에서 and using 도마에, or marking the board as the object of 썰다. Collocations: 도마 위에서 썰다, 나무 도마, 도마를 씻다, 도마 소리.

usage: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up liquid) — the exact partner verb for a ladle.
to dish out with a ladle
푸다 (scoop and serve out) is also natural: 국을 국자로 퍼서 담다.
The chain 뜨다/푸다 → 그릇에 담다 is how you serve soup with 국자.
Counted simply with 개/하나; 국자 하나 주세요 = please give me a ladle.
examples: 국자가 어디 있어요?
Where's the ladle?
Simplest frame: subject 이 + location question 어디 있다.
찌개를 국자로 떠서 그릇에 담아요.
I ladle the stew and serve it into a bowl.
Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, chained to 담다 with -서.
국이 모자라면 국자로 더 퍼서 드세요.
If there isn't enough soup, ladle out more and help yourself.
Real situation: conditional -면 + 푸다 (ㅜ-irregular) with honorific 드시다.
nuance: 국자 is the long-handled ladle for serving soup or stew — native Korean, built transparently from 국 'soup' + 자 (a tool suffix seen in 주걱 'rice paddle' family of kitchen tools). Its dedicated partner verbs are 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid) and 푸다 (to scoop-and-serve out), so a full serving action is 국을 국자로 떠서/퍼서 그릇에 담다. Don't confuse 국자 with 주걱, the flat rice paddle for scooping cooked rice — different shape, different food. Note 푸다 is a ㅜ-irregular verb: its 요-form is 퍼요 (not 푸어요), a small trap when you describe ladling. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you scoop 국자로 (instrument 으로), never 국자에. Collocations: 국자로 뜨다, 국자로 푸다, 국을 국자로 담다, 국자 하나.
